Appendix A Group convolutional neural networks

With a symmetry group denoted by GG, input denoted by xx and transformations that correspond to the group elements by gg, a function, layer or network ff is equivariant with respect to the transformations gg if

f⁡(g​x)=g′​(f⁡(x))f(gx)=g^{\prime}(f(x)) (26)

for any gg, where gg and g′g^{\prime} do not in general need to be the same. As illustrated in FIG. 10 invariance is obtained if g′g^{\prime} is identity map for all transformations gg. In other words, ff preserves the symmetry group structure in the sense that acting on inputs by symmetry transformations causes outputs to be transformed by the same symmetry elements in a non-trivial way.

For systems of interacting spins on a lattice neural network ansätze for the wavefunctions |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle of the lattice Hamiltonian associate a complex number ψ⁡(σ→,α→)\psi(\vec{\sigma};\vec{\alpha}) with each computational basis configuration of spins |σ→⟩|\vec{\sigma}\rangle where α→\vec{\alpha} denotes the network parameters:

|ψ⟩=∑{σ}→ψ⁡(σ→,α→)​|σ→⟩,|\psi\rangle=\sum_{\vec{\left\{\sigma\right\}}}\psi\left(\vec{\sigma};\vec{\alpha}\right)|\vec{\sigma}\rangle, (27)

and σ→={σ⁡(r→1),…,σ⁡(r→N)}\vec{\sigma}=\left\{\sigma(\vec{r}_{1}),...,\sigma(\vec{r}_{N})\right\} with r→1,…,r→N\vec{r}_{1},...,\vec{r}_{N} being positions of the lattice sites. Spin configurations |σ→⟩|\vec{\sigma}\rangle are the network inputs, and the complex coefficients ψ⁡(σ→)\psi(\vec{\sigma}) are the network outputs as illustrated in FIG. 11.

For example, for a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions a CNN convolutional mapping is

ψ⁡(r→)=∑r′→K⁡(r→−r′→)​σ​(r′→),\psi\left(\vec{r}\right)=\sum_{\vec{r^{\prime}}}K\left(\vec{r}-\vec{r^{\prime}}\right)\sigma\left(\vec{r^{\prime}}\right), (28)

where KK is an arbitrary kernel matrix that looks for and filters patterns in σ→\vec{\sigma}. The mapping is clearly translation equivariant since

∑r′→K⁡(r→−r′→)​σ​(r′→+t→)=∑r′→K⁡(r→+t→−r′→)​σ​(r′→)\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{r^{\prime}}}K\left(\vec{r}-\vec{r^{\prime}}\right)\sigma\left(\vec{r^{\prime}}+\vec{t}\;\right)=\sum_{\vec{r^{\prime}}}K\left(\vec{r}+\vec{t}-\vec{r^{\prime}}\right)\sigma\left(\vec{r^{\prime}}\right)
=ψ⁡(r→+t→).\displaystyle=\psi\left(\vec{r}+\vec{t}\;\right). (29)

It can similarly be shown that several iterations of convolutional mappings of the form (28) combined with arbitrary pointwise non-linear functions, and therefore neural networks built from layers of such mappings, are also translation equivariant. A translation for t→\vec{t} acts by adding t→\vec{t} to both input and output coordinates and shifting input data and then passing the data through a number of layers is the same as passing the original data through the same layers and then shifting the resulting output feature maps.

In GCNNs convolutions of the form (28) are generalized to arbitrary discrete nonabelian groups. For a symmetry group G with elements g^\hat{g} an embedding layer first generates feature maps from the input data

𝐟g1=Γ⁡(∑r→𝐊⁡(g^−1​r→)​σ​(r→))\mathbf{f}_{g}^{1}=\Gamma\left(\sum_{\vec{r}}\mathbf{K}\left(\;\hat{g}^{-1}\vec{r}\;\right)\sigma\left(\;\vec{r}\;\right)\right) (30)

for a set of learnable kernels or filters 𝐊\mathbf{K} that extract local features from the input and Γ\Gamma is a non-linear activation function. The output of the embedding layer is further passed to any number of group convolutional layers denoted by i=2,..,Nli=2,..,N_{l} where feature to feature convolutions are performed as

𝐟gi+1=Γ⁡(∑h^∈G𝐖i​(h^−1​g^)​𝐟hi)\mathbf{f}_{g}^{i+1}=\Gamma\left(\sum_{\hat{h}\in G}\mathbf{W}^{i}\left(\hat{h}^{-1}\hat{g}\right)\mathbf{f}_{h}^{i}\right) (31)

for a set of convolutional kernels 𝐖\mathbf{W}. Depth of the filters 𝐊\mathbf{K} is one (the same depth as input data) and depth of the filters 𝐖i\mathbf{W}^{i} equals to the number of feature maps in the ii-th layer. Here Γ\Gamma is taken to be scaled exponential linear unit (SELU) activation function:

SELU​(x)=a​{x​x>0b⁡(ex−1)​x≤0\mbox{SELU}(x)=a\begin{cases}x\;\;\;x>0&\\ b(e^{x}-1)\;\;\;x\leq 0\end{cases} (32)

with a≈1.05a\approx 1.05 and b≈1.67b\approx 1.67, and applied separately to the real and imaginary components:

Γ⁡(x)=SELU​(Re​(x))+i​SELU​(Im​(x)).\Gamma(x)=\mbox{SELU}(\mbox{Re}(x))+i\mbox{SELU}(\mbox{Im}(x)). (33)

The SELU activation functions were introduced for self-normalizing neural networks[167] since these activations generate self-normalizing properties, namely variance stabilization that helps in avoiding exploding and vanishing gradients when training deep neural networks, i.e. when optimizing variational wave function parameters. The SELU nonlinearity moves distribution of the nonlinearity inputs for the network layers towards mean being zero and variance one allowing stable training for very deep neural networks.

All NlN_{l} hidden layers are followed by the Γ\Gamma activation function. To obtain ψ⁡(σ)\psi(\sigma) in Eq. (27) the final output layer exponentiates complex-valued feature maps composed of two real-valued feature maps, calculates sum of these exponentiated values, and projects the sum on a particular irreducible representation of the symmetry group GG that corresponds to the symmetry properties of the ansatz wavefuntion:

ψ⁡(σ→)=∑g^∈Gχg∗​∑n=1Nfexp⁡(fn,gNl)\psi(\vec{\sigma})=\sum_{\hat{g}\in G}\chi_{g}^{*}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{f}}\exp\left(f^{N_{l}}_{n,g}\right) (34)

where NfN_{f} is the number of complex-valued feature maps (composed of 2⋅Nf2\cdot N_{f} real-valued feature maps) in the NlN_{l}-th layer and χg\chi_{g} are characters of the irreducible representation.[168, 169] The nonlinear activation function before the output is taken to be identity function.

Within group theory representations are eigenfunctions of the symmetry group operations. Irreducible representations are eigenfunctions of all group operations whilst reducible representations are eigenfunctions only of a subset of these operations. Each irreducible representation has different set of eigenvalues. These eigenvalues are characters χg\chi_{g} in the Eq. (34). For non-degenerate symmetry groups where every irreducible representation consists of one eigenfunction, characters are +1+1 or −1-1, whilst for degenerate symmetry groups characters can differ from ±1\pm 1.

Described GCNN models are significantly more expressive and yield more accurate results than standard symmetry-averaged models obtained by applying the projection formula: [168, 169]

|ψ⟩\displaystyle\left|\psi\right\rangle =\displaystyle= dχ|G|​∑g^∈Gχg∗​g^​|ψ~⟩,\displaystyle\frac{d_{\chi}}{|G|}\sum_{\hat{g}\in G}\chi_{g}^{*}\hat{g}|\;\tilde{\psi}\;\rangle, (35)
ψ⁡(σ→)\displaystyle\psi\left(\vec{\sigma}\right) =\displaystyle= dχ|G|​∑g^∈Gχg∗​ψ~​(g^−1​σ→),\displaystyle\frac{d_{\chi}}{|G|}\sum_{\hat{g}\in G}\chi_{g}^{*}\tilde{\psi}\left(\hat{g}^{-1}\vec{\sigma}\right),

where |G||G| is the order of the group GG (the number of its elements) and dχd_{\chi} is dimension of the irreducible representation with characters χg\chi_{g}. The projection symmetry averaging approach has been applied to various ansatz wavefunctions[113, 78, 76, 115, 71] and requires evaluation of the model ψ~\tilde{\psi} for all symmetry related basis states which can be very computationally expensive. These models are also equivariant with respect to the symmetry group GG which can be seen by rewriting an ansatz of the form (35) as an equivariant model with the output dimension |G||G|:

ψg​(σ→)\displaystyle\psi_{g}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right) ≡\displaystyle\equiv ψ~​(g^−1​σ→),\displaystyle\tilde{\psi}\left(\hat{g}^{-1}\vec{\sigma}\right), (36)
ψg​(h^−1​σ→)\displaystyle\psi_{g}\left(\hat{h}^{-1}\vec{\sigma}\right) =\displaystyle= ψ~​(g^−1​h^−1​σ→)=ψh​g​(σ→).\displaystyle\tilde{\psi}\left(\hat{g}^{-1}\hat{h}^{-1}\vec{\sigma}\right)=\psi_{hg}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right).

Within this formulation all ψg​(σ→)\psi_{g}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right) can be obtained by evaluating the equivariant model for a single input and symmetrization is equivalent to averaging over the model output which is computationally preferable.

For example, for the simpler square lattice with periodic boundary conditions the projection formula (35) becomes familiar Fourier transform that finds crystal momentum eigenstates:

ψ(σ→)=1Lx⋅Ly∑r→e−ik→⋅r→ψr→(σ→),\psi\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)=\frac{1}{L_{x}\cdot L_{y}}\sum_{\vec{r}}e^{-i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}}\psi_{\vec{r}}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right), (37)

with LxL_{x} and LyL_{y} being the lattice dimensions and k→=2​π⋅(nx/Lx,ny/Ly)\vec{k}=2\pi\cdot\left(n_{x}/L_{x},n_{y}/L_{y}\right), nq∈{0,…,Lq−1}n_{q}\in\left\{0,...,L_{q}-1\right\}, q∈{x,y}q\in\left\{x,y\right\}. Irreducible representations of the translation group are therefore one-dimensional and can be labeled by the phases ei​k→⋅r→e^{i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}}.

GCNNs can be mapped to other deep neural network models with symmetry averaging by masking filters, i.e. by setting various off-diagonal feature-to-feature filters (convolution kernels WW) to zero whilst keeping the input-to-feature filters (embedding kernels KK) the same. [80, 81] Diagonal filters are filters with h^=g^\hat{h}=\hat{g} in (4) and off-diagonal filters are obtained for h^≠g^\hat{h}\neq\hat{g}. For example translationally equivariant CNN model symmetry averaged over a lattice point group symmetries can be obtained by masking off-diagonal filters that correspond to point group rotations and reflections. This model would be more restrictive than a GCNN model equivariant with respect to all space-group symmetries yielding less accurate results.[119, 80, 81]

It should be noted that the described procedure of constructing the wave-function ansätze equivariant with respect to a discrete symmetry group cannot straightforwardly be generalized to continuous symmetry groups like S​U​(2)SU(2) spin rotation symmetry. Finding efficient ways to introduce continuous symmetries is still an open research problem with one of the possible solutions being sampling in the basis of irreducible representations instead of spins.[97, 98, 113]

Appendix B Training scheme and wave-function optimization

The goal of VMC is to find the optimal set of (complex) parameters α→={α1,…,αNp}\vec{\alpha}=\left\{\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{N_{p}}\right\} in an ansatz wavefunction of the form (27) that minimizes a suitably chosen loss function. The standard optimization technique is the gradient descent (GD) method within which the parameters are updated according to the gradients of the chosen loss function with the iterative update rule

α→t+1=α→t−η​∇→α→​ℒ,\vec{\alpha}_{t+1}=\vec{\alpha}_{t}-\eta\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\mathcal{L}, (38)

where tt denotes iteration, η\eta is the learning rate (the step size) and ℒ\mathcal{L} is a loss function. All numerical methods that attempt to find a global minimum using local information for iterative parameter updates generally exhibit problems related to the local minima in the loss function landscape and slow convergence. Various stochastic methods are therefore introduced to help mentioned numerical algorithms to escape local minima and improve convergence, for example Adam[140] and natural gradient descent (NGD) method.[170, 171, 172, 173, 174, 175]

In the Eq. (38) -∇→α→​ℒ\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\mathcal{L} represent directions in which the parameters can be updated to obtain the largest decrease of the loss function. The parameters are adjusted by a small step length, i.e. moved for a small distance in the parameter space, in the direction determined by the gradient to optimize the loss function. The standard GD and NGD methods differ by how a small distance is defined. Whilst in the standard GD distance is Euclidean distance that corresponds to the flat metric on the parameter manifold, NGD replaces the flat metric by a generally non-flat metric. NGD method takes into account that changes of all parameters can not be treated equally and that it is not always correct to define distance in terms of how much the parameters are adjusted. Instead a change for each parameter has to be scaled according to the effect of the change on the neural network output distribution.

To define a new form of distance that accounts for relationships between parameters and reflects changes in the network output distribution NGD method introduces a metric matrix MM

α→t+1=α→t−η​M−1​∇→α→​ℒ,\vec{\alpha}_{t+1}=\vec{\alpha}_{t}-\eta M^{-1}\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\mathcal{L}, (39)

In the context of VMC with neural networks NGD method corresponds to the stochastic reconfiguration method (SR),[68, 132, 133, 134, 135, 175] where the Hilbert-space distance dd between two unnormalized wavefunctions |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle and |ϕ′⟩|\phi^{\prime}\rangle is given by the Fubini-Study metrics:

dF​S=arccos⁡⟨ϕ′|ϕ⟩​⟨ϕ|ϕ′⟩⟨ϕ′|ϕ′⟩​⟨ϕ|ϕ⟩.\mbox{d}_{FS}=\arccos\sqrt{\frac{\langle\phi^{\prime}|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|\phi^{\prime}\rangle}{\langle\phi^{\prime}|\phi^{\prime}\rangle\langle\phi|\phi\rangle}}. (40)

Within SR the parameter updates (39) at each iteration tt can be obtained by applying imaginary time evolution operator e−Δ​τ​ℒ≈1−Δ​τ​ℒe^{-\Delta\tau\mathcal{L}}\approx 1-\Delta\tau\mathcal{L} to the ansatz wavefunction at imaginary time τ\tau:

|ψ′​(α→​(τ))⟩=(1−Δ​τ​ℒ)​|ψ⁡(α→​(τ))⟩,|\psi^{\prime}\left(\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau\right)\right)\rangle=\left(1-\Delta\tau\mathcal{L}\right)|\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau\right)\right)\rangle, (41)

where Δ​τ\Delta\tau is a small imaginary time step that corresponds to the learning rate η\eta in the Eq. (39). After each imaginary time step Δ​τ\Delta\tau the wavefunction |ψ′​(α→​(τ))⟩|\psi^{\prime}\left(\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau\right)\right)\rangle is projected to the variational subspace by minimizing dF​S2d_{FS}^{2} with |ϕ⟩=|ψ⁡(α→​(τ))⟩+Δ​τ​∂τψ⁡(α→​(τ))|\phi\rangle=|\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau\right)\right)\rangle+\Delta\tau\partial_{\tau}\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau\right)\right) and |ϕ′⟩=|ψ′​(α→​(τ))⟩|\phi^{\prime}\rangle=|\psi^{\prime}\left(\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau\right)\right)\rangle in the Eq. (40) to obtain a new set of parameters α→t+1≡α→​(τ+Δ​τ)\vec{\alpha}_{t+1}\equiv\vec{\alpha}\left(\tau+\Delta\tau\right):

α→t+1=α→t−Δ​τ​G−1​∇→α→​ℒ,\vec{\alpha}_{t+1}=\vec{\alpha}_{t}-\Delta\tau G^{-1}\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\mathcal{L}, (42)

where the metric matrix MM corresponds to the quantum geometric tensor (QGT):

Gi​j=⟨∂αiψ⁡(α→)|∂αjψ⁡(α→)⟩⟨ψ⁡(α→)|ψ⁡(α→)⟩\displaystyle G_{ij}=\frac{\langle\partial_{\alpha_{i}}\psi(\vec{\alpha})|\partial_{\alpha_{j}}\psi(\vec{\alpha})\rangle}{\langle\psi(\vec{\alpha})|\psi(\vec{\alpha})\rangle} (43)
−⟨∂αiψ⁡(α→)​|ψ⁡(α→)⟩​⟨ψ⁡(α→)|​∂αjψ⁡(α→)⟩⟨ψ⁡(α→)|ψ⁡(α→)⟩2,\displaystyle-\frac{\langle\partial_{\alpha_{i}}\psi(\vec{\alpha})|\psi(\vec{\alpha})\rangle\langle\psi(\vec{\alpha})|\partial_{\alpha_{j}}\psi(\vec{\alpha})\rangle}{\langle\psi(\vec{\alpha})|\psi(\vec{\alpha})\rangle^{2}},

and ∂αi=∂/∂αi\partial_{\alpha_{i}}=\partial/\partial\alpha_{i} are partial derivatives with respect to the network parameters α→={α1,…,αNp}\vec{\alpha}=\left\{\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{N_{p}}\right\}. The QGT is also often called the S matrix or quantum Fisher matrix in analogy to the classical Fisher information matrix.[65, 66, 175, 170, 174] Schematic illustration of the imaginary time evolution in the SR method is shown in FIG. 12.

The loss function in VMC can for example be the variational energy:

ℒE≡E=⟨ψ⁡(α→)|H|ψ⁡(α→)⟩⟨ψ⁡(α→)|ψ⁡(α→)⟩.\mathcal{L}_{E}\equiv E=\frac{\langle\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\right)|H|\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\right)\rangle}{\langle\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\right)|\psi\left(\vec{\alpha}\right)\rangle}. (44)

where HH is the Hamiltonian of the system or free energy at temperature TT:

ℒF≡F=E−T​S,\mathcal{L}_{F}\equiv F=E-TS, (45)

where the entropy is defined as[80, 81, 136, 137, 138, 139]

S=−∑σ→|ψ⁡(σ→,α→)|2∑σ′→|ψ⁡(σ′→,α→)|2log|ψ⁡(σ→,α→)|2∑σ′→|ψ⁡(σ′→,α→)|2,S=-\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\frac{|\psi\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\right)|^{2}}{\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}|\psi\left(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}},\vec{\alpha}\right)|^{2}}\log\frac{|\psi\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\right)|^{2}}{\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}|\psi\left(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}},\vec{\alpha}\right)|^{2}}, (46)

and ψ⁡(σ→,α→)\psi\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\right) is an unnormalized neural-network ansatz wavefunction.

Minimizing the free energy loss function (45) corresponds to minimizing Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence that measures closeness between two distributions. For a statistical physics model the joint probability for spins σ→={σ1,…,σN}\vec{\sigma}=\left\{\sigma_{1},...,\sigma_{N}\right\} follows the Boltzmann distribution

p⁡(σ→)=e−β​E​(σ→)Z,p\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)=\frac{e^{-\beta E\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)}}{Z}, (47)

where β=1/T\beta=1/T is the inverse temperature and ZZ is the partition function and the free energy ℱ\mathcal{F} can be obtained as ℱ=−lnZ/β\mathcal{F}=-\ln Z/\beta. The KL divergence[176]

DK​L=∑σ→ψ⁡(α→,σ→)​ln⁡(ψ⁡(α→,σ→)p⁡(σ→))=β⁡(F−ℱ)D_{KL}=\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\psi\left(\vec{\alpha},\vec{\sigma}\right)\ln\left(\frac{\psi\left(\vec{\alpha},\vec{\sigma}\right)}{p\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)}\right)=\beta\left(F-\mathcal{F}\right) (48)

then measures closeness between the Boltzmann distribution p⁡(σ→)p(\vec{\sigma}) and ψ⁡(α→,σ→)\psi\left(\vec{\alpha},\vec{\sigma}\right) distribution parameterized by variational parameters α→\vec{\alpha} where

F=1β∑σ→ψ(α→,σ→)[βE(σ→)+lnψ(α→,σ→))]F=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\psi\left(\vec{\alpha},\vec{\sigma}\right)\left[\beta E\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)+\ln\psi\left(\vec{\alpha},\vec{\sigma}\right))\right] (49)

is the variational free energy that gives an upper bound for the free energy ℱ\mathcal{F}. Since the KL divergence is non-negative, KL minimization is equivalent to the free energy loss (45) minimization.

Within the VMC algorithm the quantum expectation value of any operator A^\hat{A}

⟨A^⟩=⟨ψ|A^|ψ⟩⟨ψ|ψ⟩\langle\hat{A}\rangle=\frac{\langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle}{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle} (50)

can be efficiently evaluated by rewriting the expectation value as a Monte Carlo average

⟨A^⟩=∑σ→P⁡(σ→)​Al​o​c​(σ→)≈1Ns​∑σ→Al​o​c​(σ→)\langle\hat{A}\rangle=\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}P\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right)A^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right)\approx\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}A^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right) (51)

with respect to the quantum probability distribution

P⁡(σ→)=|⟨σ→|ψ⟩|2⟨ψ|ψ⟩P\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right)=\frac{|\langle\vec{\sigma}\;|\psi\rangle|^{2}}{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle} (52)

and estimating the average from NsN_{s} samples obtained using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling methods that generate a sequence of NsN_{s} samples that asymptotically follow distribution P⁡(σ→)P(\vec{\sigma}\;), where the local estimator Al​o​c​(σ→)A^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right) is

Al​o​c​(σ→)=⟨σ→|A^|ψ⟩⟨σ→|ψ⟩=∑σ′→ψ⁡(σ′→)ψ⁡(σ→)​⟨σ→|A^|σ′→⟩.A^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)=\frac{\langle\vec{\sigma}\;|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle}{\langle\vec{\sigma}\;|\psi\rangle}=\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}\frac{\psi(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}\;)}{\psi\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right)}\langle\vec{\sigma}\;|\hat{A}|\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}\;\rangle. (53)

Starting from the set of kernels within all layers initialized with Lecun normal initializer that draws samples from a truncated normal distribution centered on zero that gives correct variance of the output,[167] initial parameter values are updated within the SR algorithm at each iteration according to Eq. (42) with the free energy loss function described by Eq. (45) and the QGT regularization as in Eq. (43). The QGT and the free energy loss function gradient can also be efficiently evaluated as Monte Carlo averages. Whilst the free energy loss in Eq. (45) can not be efficiently evaluated from the MCMC samples since our calculations are performed with unnormalized neural-network ansatz wavefunctions and the entropy in Eq. (46) therefore can not be calculated, the loss function gradient within the VMC scheme can be evaluated from

∇→α→​S\displaystyle\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}S =\displaystyle= −∑σ→P(σ→,α→)lnp(σ→,α→)[∇→α→lnp(σ→,α→)\displaystyle-\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}P\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)\ln p\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)[\;\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\ln p\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right) (54)
−\displaystyle- ∑σ′→P(σ′→,α→)∇→α→lnp(σ′→,α→)]\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}P(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}},\vec{\alpha}\;)\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\ln p(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}},\vec{\alpha}\;)\;]
≈\displaystyle\approx −1Ns∑σ→lnp(σ→,α→)[∇→α→lnp(σ→,α→)\displaystyle-\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\ln p\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)[\;\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\ln p\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)
−\displaystyle- 1Ns∑σ′→∇→α→lnp(σ′→,α→)],\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\ln p(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}},\vec{\alpha}\;)\;],

where P⁡(σ→,α→)P\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\right) is the probability distribution (52), p⁡(σ→,α→)=|ψ⁡(σ→,α→)|2p\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)=|\psi\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)|^{2}, log⁡p=2​Re​ln⁡ψ\log p=2\mbox{Re}\ln\psi and

∇→α→​E=2​Re​[f→]\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}E=2\mbox{Re}[\vec{f}] (55)

with f→\vec{f} being

f→\displaystyle\vec{f} =\displaystyle= ∑σ→P(σ→,α→)O→∗(σ→)[El​o​c(σ→)\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}P\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\;\right)\vec{O}^{*}\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right)[\;E^{loc}(\vec{\sigma}) (56)
−\displaystyle- ∑σ′→P(σ′→,α→)El​o​c(σ′→))]\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}P(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}},\vec{\alpha}\;)E^{loc}(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}))\;]
≈\displaystyle\approx 1Ns∑σ→O→∗(σ→)[El​o​c(σ→)−1Ns∑σ′→El​o​c(σ′→))]\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\vec{O}^{*}\left(\vec{\sigma}\;\right)[\;E^{loc}(\vec{\sigma})-\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}}E^{loc}(\vec{\sigma^{\prime}}))\;]

and O→=∇→α→​ln⁡ψ⁡(σ,α→)\vec{O}=\vec{\nabla}_{\vec{\alpha}}\ln\psi\left(\sigma,\vec{\alpha}\right) the gradient of log-amplitudes. We note that Eq. (55) is valid for non-holomorphic mapping α→→ψ⁡(σ→,α→)\vec{\alpha}\rightarrow\psi\left(\vec{\sigma},\vec{\alpha}\right) where Re​[αi]\mbox{Re}[\alpha_{i}] and Im​[αi]\mbox{Im}[\alpha_{i}] can be treated as two independent real parameters and Eq. (55) can be applied to each separately.

Additionally correlators of the form ⟨A^​B^⟩\langle\hat{A}\hat{B}\rangle can be the most efficiently evaluated as covariance of the local estimators for A^\hat{A} and B^\hat{B}:

⟨A^​B^⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{A}\hat{B}\rangle =\displaystyle= ⟨ψ|A^​B^|ψ⟩⟨ψ|ψ⟩=∑σ→P⁡(σ→)​[Al​o​c​(σ→)]∗​Bl​o​c​(σ→)\displaystyle\frac{\langle\psi|\hat{A}\hat{B}|\psi\rangle}{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}=\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}P\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)\left[A^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)\right]^{*}B^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right) (57)
≈\displaystyle\approx 1Ns​∑σ→[Al​o​c​(σ→)]∗​Bl​o​c​(σ→)\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\left[A^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)\right]^{*}B^{loc}\left(\vec{\sigma}\right)

where P⁡(σ→)P\left(\vec{\sigma}\right) is the probability distribution in Eq. (52).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
